summary: Identifies protocols and applications that break when a NAT sits in the path, and notes known workarounds. It is not exhaustive. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A front desk that rewrites labels on mail can confuse programs that write their return address inside the letter. This lists which programs get confused.

subtitle: A catalogue of the protocols and applications that break when a NAT sits in the path, with known workarounds.

tldr.problem: A Network Address Translator (NAT) rewrites addresses in IP headers, but many applications also carry addresses or ports inside their payload or depend on connections in a direction the NAT does not allow.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the common traits of protocols that break, then goes through specific protocols: those that cannot work with NAT, those that can work with an Application Level Gateway (ALG), and one designed to work with NAT.
tldr.outcome: It is a non-exhaustive Informational survey meant to give clues for applications it does not cover. It does not advocate NAT.

today: RFC 3027 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a snapshot from January 2001 of applications known to have trouble with NAT, and it points to RFC 3022 for Traditional NAT.

sections.title: Scope and Approach
sections.content:
Many applications are hurt when the two end nodes are in different address realms and a NAT in the path bridges them. The NAT alone cannot give every application transparency, so it may be helped by an Application Level Gateway (ALG), which is application specific and likely has to examine and recompose the IP payload.

The document lists protocols known to be affected by NAT in the path. The authors state that it is a subset, not a comprehensive list, and that it is not intended to advocate NAT. It assumes the reader knows NAT terminology from RFC 2663 and mainly addresses Traditional NAT, especially NAPT (RFC 3022).
sections.eli5: A NAT is a helper that swaps labels on packets. Sometimes a second helper, an ALG, has to read the letter inside as well. This memo lists who needs the second helper.

sections.title: Common Traits of Broken Protocols
sections.content:
The memo names six characteristics that tend to break under NAT:

  • Realm-specific addresses in the payload. An ALG may help, but if the payload is secured with IPsec or another security mechanism, the application is bound to fail.
  • Bundled sessions such as FTP, H.323, SIP and RTSP, where a control connection sets up data flows. NAT treats each session as unrelated, and the data session may start in a direction NAT does not permit.
  • Peer-to-peer applications, where a session from outside is as likely as one from inside. A suggested workaround for Traditional NAT is for private hosts to keep an outbound connection to a server that represents them on the global Internet.
  • IP fragmentation with NAPT. Two private hosts sending fragmented TCP/UDP packets to one destination with the same fragmentation identifier cannot be told apart, so both sessions are corrupted.
  • Needing an address mapping retained across consecutive sessions, which NAT cannot know.
  • Needing more public addresses than exist. The example is rlogin, which uses well-known port 512, so no more than one private host can use the service at a time.
sections.eli5: NAT gets confused when a program writes its own address inside the message, opens a second channel back to you, or needs a separate public address for every user.

sections.title: Protocols That Cannot Work With NAT
sections.content:
The memo says end-to-end IPsec is, for all practical purposes, impossible with NAT in the path. IPsec AH is designed to detect changes to the IP header, so a packet whose address NAT rewrote is invalidated. With ESP in transport mode, the TCP/UDP header is encrypted, so NAT cannot update the checksum and the receiver will fail checksum validation. IKE can carry IP addresses as identifiers in payloads that are hashed or encrypted.

Kerberos 4 and Kerberos 5 tickets are encrypted, so no ALG can be written. Tickets are tied to the requesting IP address, so with NAPT the ticket is valid from any host inside the private realm, which weakens security. For Kerberos 5 the workarounds (listing the NAPT address, or removing all addresses from the ticket) both reduce ticket security.

The X Window System sends its DISPLAY variable with a local IP address inline during Telnet negotiation, and its client/server roles are reversed from most applications. RSH sends a random port number inline for a stderr connection that goes back from server to client, and unlike FTP has no PASV equivalent. Kerberos-protected RSH and RLOGIN fail for the ticket reasons above.
sections.eli5: Some programs lock their letters in a sealed envelope that the helper is not allowed to open. If the helper changes the address on the outside, the receiver says the letter was tampered with.

sections.title: Protocols That Can Work With an ALG
sections.content:
These protocols can work if an ALG rewrites the addresses inside their payload, and the memo notes where encryption or authentication defeats that.

  • FTP: the control session uses well-known port 21, and the PORT and PASV commands can change data ports. An ALG must rewrite those and also fix sequence and acknowledgement numbers, checksums and packet length. If the control channel is secured, the ALG cannot do this.
  • RSVP: messages can contain IP addresses, and an RSVP Integrity object stops an ALG from altering them.
  • DNS: a DNS-ALG converts addresses and names in queries and responses, and fails if DNSSEC protects the packets. If a host just uses an external name server, no ALG is needed.
  • SMTP: mail to a server inside the private domain must be redirected from its external address; some messages carry IP addresses in Received: fields.
  • SIP: responses need not go to the request's source port, and SDP and URLs inside messages carry addresses. A SIP-ALG or a SIP proxy beside the NAT is needed.
  • RealAudio: control uses TCP port 7070 and audio returns on UDP ports 6970-7170, so it is broken by default on Traditional NAT. Bi-directional NAT needs no ALG.
  • H.323: many connections and dynamic ports, with addresses exchanged inside ASN.1-encoded data, so an H.323-ALG must decode and translate it.
  • SNMP: payloads can contain addresses; an SNMP ALG cannot be made fully transparent and fails with SNMPv3 security unless it holds the keys. SNMP proxies are an alternative.
sections.eli5: Most of these programs can still work if a second helper reads each letter and rewrites any return address written inside. If the letter is sealed, even that helper cannot do it.

sections.title: A Protocol Designed for NAT
sections.content:
The one protocol the memo describes as designed explicitly to work with NAT is the proprietary, UDP-based Activision Games protocol. An address server in the global realm, using UDP port 21157, learns each player's private address and port from the connect message, and the external address from the IP and UDP headers. It sends both to the other players, who try direct connections and use whichever address works first.

This works as long as the NAT keeps the same private-to-external binding while the player is in session, and an NAPT must allow multiple simultaneous UDP connections on the same assigned global address and port. A drawback is that a client may contact a private address that is in use locally by something else; unexpected messages are expected to be dropped.
sections.eli5: This game asks a helper who knows both your home address and your public address, then shares both with your friends. Your friends try each one until a message gets through.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says the security considerations in RFC 2663 apply to all NAT devices and that this document adds none. Security-related breakage, such as IPsec, Kerberos tickets and SNMPv3, is discussed within the protocol sections above.
sections.eli5: The memo just points back to the safety notes in an earlier NAT document.

viz.caption: SIX TRAITS THAT BREAK UNDER NAT

items.title: Addresses in payload
items.text: Realm-specific IP address or port information inside the data.

items.title: Bundled sessions
items.text: A control connection sets up separate data sessions.

items.title: Peer-to-peer
items.text: Sessions may start from either side.

items.title: Fragmentation
items.text: Same fragmentation id from two private hosts corrupts both sessions.

items.title: Retained mapping
items.text: Address mapping must survive between sessions.

items.title: Too few addresses
items.text: More private hosts than public addresses.
